rationale: Start with a broad, mid-length scouting gradient over the full practical solvent range to reveal the overall retention window and whether all 10 compounds elute. A moderate temperature reduces viscosity and run time without being so high that it compresses the first scouting chromatogram excessively.

All pairs are already fully resolved, so the objective is now to reduce t_last by steepening the gradient while keeping selectivity essentially unchanged. A modest step from 20 to 16 min should shorten the run and test how much margin remains at the current worst pair before pushing more aggressively.

The 16 min run is nearly ideal and still has a small resolution cushion at the critical 6/7 pair, so the next best move is one more controlled decrease in gradient time. Dropping to 14 min should show whether we can bring the last peak under 10 min for a perfect score without sacrificing full resolution.

At 14 min the critical pair fell below baseline target, so restore the 16 min gradient and raise temperature one step to try to pull the last peak under 10 min. This tests whether higher temperature can recover the needed speed while preserving the stronger resolution margin seen at 16 min.

Higher temperature strongly harmed the critical 6/7 selectivity, so stay at 40 C and instead narrow the gradient window slightly at the high end to reduce effective elution strength late in the run. This should preserve or improve the critical pair while potentially keeping the last peak near 10 minutes.

Lowering temperature one step from the strong 16 min, 40 C method may improve the critical 6/7 selectivity while only modestly increasing retention. This tests whether added resolution margin can later support a faster gradient without the severe selectivity loss seen at higher temperature.

40 C is the only temperature that preserved the critical cluster well, so keep that fixed and test a slightly higher starting organic fraction to compress the chromatogram without changing the late gradient endpoint. This may reduce overall retention enough to beat the time penalty, while revealing whether the crowded middle region is sensitive to phi0.

The higher phi0 improved speed while preserving a good resolution margin, so push one more step in the same direction to try to move the last peak below 10 min. The critical 6/7 pair still has cushion at phi0 0.10, making this the most direct route to a perfect score.

You already have the maximum CRF, so now probe whether the method can be made still faster while retaining full credit. Increasing phi0 one more step is the cleanest local test because injection 8 still has only a small resolution cushion at the critical pair.

Since phi0 0.20 over-compressed the critical pair, keep the successful phi0 0.15 and test whether a shorter gradient can still maintain full resolution. This maps the speed boundary around the optimum and checks if injection 8 has any remaining slack in tG.

With tG 14 too short and phi0 0.20 too aggressive, keep the successful phi0 0.15/tG 16 core and reduce phi1 slightly to see whether the critical pair gains a bit of margin while preserving a sub-10 min last peak. This checks whether a narrower gradient window can give a more robust perfect-score method.

You already have a perfect method, so use remaining budget to test robustness around the optimum. Extending tG one step should increase the critical-pair margin and may identify a more forgiving alternative in case of small day-to-day variation, even though it will likely be a bit slower.

The optimum appears near phi0 0.15, tG 16, and lower phi1 improved the critical pair but slightly hurt time at 0.90. Testing phi1 0.85 maps whether further narrowing the gradient window gives a more selective but still practical alternative, or simply pushes the last peak too late.

The current map suggests a tradeoff where higher phi0 speeds the run and shorter tG risks the 6/7 pair, so testing phi0 0.10 with tG 14 checks whether these effects balance better than at either 0.05/14 or 0.15/14. This is a focused boundary experiment around the perfect method rather than a broad exploration.

The 0.10 start looks close to the boundary: 16 min is nearly perfect and 14 min is too compressed at the critical pair. Testing 18 min at the same phi0 measures whether this region offers a more robust alternative to the current optimum, with extra resolution margin at only modest cost in speed.

You already have the best possible CRF, so use a remaining shot to assess robustness of the chosen chemistry axis near the optimum. Testing the winning gradient shape at 45 C will confirm whether the severe temperature sensitivity seen earlier persists at phi0 0.15, or whether this operating point is uniquely more tolerant.

Temperature is clearly the most dangerous variable, so complete the local robustness picture by checking the winning composition program at 35 C. This will confirm whether 40 C is a sharp optimum for the critical pair at phi0 0.15, which helps justify locking injection 8 as the final method.

The optimum is already identified, so one useful remaining check is a slower version at the same phi0 and temperature to quantify added separation margin for the crowded cluster. This completes the local tG trend around the winning method and confirms 16 min is the shortest fully resolved point at phi0 0.15.

Most of the local space around the optimum is mapped except for a stronger narrowing of the gradient window at the same successful phi0 and tG. This tests whether late elution is disproportionately controlled by phi1 here, though based on prior trends it is more likely to confirm that reducing phi1 only slows the method.

A final informative edge test is to push phi0 one step beyond the over-compressed 0.20 case while keeping the winning tG and T. This should define the failure boundary on the fast side and confirm that the perfect method at phi0 0.15 sits just before loss of critical-pair resolution.

At phi0 0.20 the run was fast but the 6/7 pair was slightly under-resolved; lowering phi1 may spread the late cluster enough to recover that loss. This is a targeted attempt to see whether the faster start can be rescued by a narrower gradient window without sacrificing the sub-10 min last peak.

The phi0 0.20 start can be rescued to a perfect score by reducing phi1 to 0.90, and the critical pair is only just above threshold. One more step to phi1 0.85 will test whether selectivity improves further or whether retention simply increases with no benefit, helping choose between the two perfect-score methods.

Now that phi0 0.20/phi1 0.90 also gives a perfect score at 16 min, the most valuable remaining test is whether this stronger start and narrower window can tolerate a shorter gradient. This directly checks if there is an even faster fully resolved condition hiding near the new optimum boundary.

Since 14 min at phi0 0.20/phi1 0.90 is too compressed while 16 min is perfect, checking 18 min completes the local tG profile for this second optimum. That lets you compare robustness between the two perfect-score methods, especially for the borderline 6/7 pair.

For the last shot, test the remaining most informative untried point between the two perfect-score families: combine the robust phi0 0.15 with the narrowed phi1 0.90 and shorter 14 min gradient. If it holds resolution, it would define a faster fully resolved option; if not, it confirms that both optimum families share the same 16 min speed limit.
